diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $\alpha > 0$. Then the functional $J : H^1(\Omega) \to \R$ in Definition \ref{def:cost_functional} has a unique global minimum.
\underset{\varepsilon \in \mathcal{E}}{\text{minimise}} \quad J(c(\,\cdot\, ,T; \varepsilon)) \quad \text{subject to \eqref{eq:MAsystem}-\eqref{eq:ellipsoid}}.
A minimiser $\varepsilon^*\in \mathcal{E}$ of $J$ is called an \textit{optimal control} and the evolution of the multi-agent system associated with it is the optimal trajectory.
Due to the non-linearity of the ODE system \eqref{eq:MAsystem}, the control-to-state map $\varepsilon \mapsto c(\,\cdot\, ,T; \varepsilon)$ is not convex.

Section \ref{sec:OCP} is dedicated to the first optimal control formulation. We define a cost functional based on the $L^2$ norm of the intensity gradient, establish the well-posedness of the problem, and derive the corresponding optimality system.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper presents the well-posedness of 'the problem' as established in the section devoted to the Mayer optimal control problem (eq:OCP) and names its minimizers 'optimal controls', but the only existence/uniqueness theorem proved (thm:existence1) concerns the static functional J : H^1 -> R. No existence result for the Mayer problem is given: the control space of measurable functions into a compact set E is not compact in any topology under which the control-to-state map is continuous (the map is non-convex, and weak-* limits of controls are not preserved through the nonlinear kernel), so the Direct Method does not apply and the advertised well-posedness is unsupported.

failure_location.quote: The following result ensures the well-posedness of the problem

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Scope the well-posedness claim to the static cost functional (local rewording), or add an existence theorem for eq:OCP via compactness plus continuity of the control-to-state map (possibly in a relaxed control space), which is a new argument.
issues.overall_effect: The Mayer problem's central guarantee (existence of an optimal control) is assumed rather than established; the optimality system and both algorithms are derived for a problem whose solvability is never proved. No labelled theorem is invalidated, since none asserts the Mayer problem's existence.
issues.title: Well-posedness is advertised for the Mayer control problem but only the static cost functional is proved well-posed
issues.why_classification: The least adequate repair is a local clarification preserving every theorem, algorithm, and numerical conclusion; the gap is real but nothing formal depends on it.

issues.failure_explanation: With the terminal condition stated in eq:opt_system-b (lambda(T) = J'(c(T)), the standard Pontryagin convention), the sensitivity identity gives grad J = integral of (dF/deps)^T lambda, so D^(j) = dF/deps . lambda^(j) is the gradient of J. The Armijo test in Algorithm alg:dal correctly probes descent steps eps - tau D, but the update applies eps + sigma D, the opposite direction: as written the algorithm performs gradient ascent on J, not the advertised steepest descent. The sign convention is also inconsistent across the paper: the augmented cost eq:augmented_cost uses +lambda[dc/dt - F], whose stationarity in c forces lambda(T) = -J'(c(T)) = Delta c(T) - alpha(c(T)-I), the negative of the stated terminal condition (the appendix's own integration-by-parts display confirms this opposite sign), while the appendix's discrete functional gradient drops the minus sign present in J'(eps)[z] = - integral lambda dF/deps z. At least one of the three sign choices (augmented cost, terminal condition, update/line-search directions) must be reversed; as written they cannot all be correct.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reverse one sign consistently: keep the Pontryagin terminal condition and the Armijo test and change the update to eps - sigma D, and reconcile the augmented-cost sign in eq:augmented_cost and the appendix; all guarantees then survive.
issues.overall_effect: Algorithm alg:dal does not minimize J as written (it ascends); Algorithm alg:admm, which calls alg:dal on its third line, inherits the defect; the terminal condition of eq:opt_system and the augmented cost eq:augmented_cost are mutually inconsistent, and all numerical conclusions of Sections 3.2 and 4 presuppose the corrected sign.
issues.title: DAL update applies the gradient-ascent direction while the Armijo search probes descent; the adjoint sign convention contradicts the augmented cost
issues.why_classification: The repair is a single sign reversal plus a convention alignment; it is local and routine and loses no mathematical content, rate, or guarantee.

issues.failure_explanation: When the initial step sigma^(j) already satisfies the Armijo condition, the loop increases tau by the factor 1/b while the condition holds and stops at the first tau^(k) for which it fails; the algorithm then sets sigma^(j+1) = tau^(k), accepting a step that violates the sufficient-decrease condition instead of the last successful step tau^(k-1). The two branches are asymmetric: the decrease branch correctly stops at the first step satisfying Armijo, while the increase branch stops at the first step violating it. The accepted step can fail to decrease J sufficiently (or at all, once projected onto E).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Accept the last Armijo-satisfying step (sigma^(j+1) = tau^(k-1)) in the increase branch; a one-line correction.
issues.overall_effect: The line search's sufficient-decrease guarantee fails on the step-increase branch, undermining the descent argument and the stationarity-based stopping criterion; the defect propagates to Algorithm alg:admm, which nests alg:dal. issues.title: Two-way Armijo line search accepts the first step-size violating sufficient decrease in the step-increase branch
issues.why_classification: A one-line bookkeeping correction restores the line-search guarantee with no loss of content.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where the compactly supported interaction kernel is given by the $C^2$ Wendland function \cite{Wendland1995}
In particular, each agent tends to align its state $c_i$ with the states of nearby agents whose intensities are similar, while the strength of this influence decays with spatial distance.
This behaviour can be encoded by an interaction kernel which quantifies the attraction between two agents as a function of both their spatial and tonal distances.

When $\phi$ has compact support, the interaction domain is a bounded ellipsoid in $[0,1]^3$, centred at $p_i$ and with semi–axes proportional to $(\varepsilon_x(t)^{-1/2}, \varepsilon_x(t)^{-1/2}, \varepsilon_c(t)^{-1/2})$.
Classical results for opinion dynamics models~\cite{MotschTadmor2014} ensure that, under mild assumptions on $\phi$, the solution converges to a finite number of clusters in finite time.

issues.failure_explanation: The standard C^2 Wendland kernel (Wendland 1995, as used in SPH, cf. Dehnen 2012) is phi(r) = (1-r)^4 (4r+1) on [0,1]: positive, with phi(0) = 1 and phi'(0) = 0. The printed kernel (4r-1)(1-r)^4 equals -1 at r = 0 (so it is discontinuous at 0, being 0 for r < 0), is negative on [0,1/4), attains its maximum (3/5)^5 at r = 2/5, and has phi'(0) = 8, not 0. With the printed kernel, pairs with r_ij < 1/4 interact with negative weight, i.e. they repel instead of aligning; the 'interaction domain' is an ellipsoidal shell rather than the ellipsoid described in the text, and the 'mild assumptions on phi' (e.g. nonnegativity) behind the cited clustering results are violated. The single forced correction is 4r-1 -> 4r+1, which restores the cited Wendland kernel; all formulas involving phi (eq:dF_dc, eq:dF_depsx, eq:dF_depsc) are written for a general phi and survive the correction.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace (4r-1) by (4r+1) in eq:kernel; no other change is needed since every use of phi is symbolic.
issues.overall_effect: The multi-agent dynamics eq:MAsystem as printed does not implement attraction/alignment (repulsive core for close pairs); the geometric description of the interaction domain and the clustering justification are invalidated, and the numerical experiments are affected unless the implemented kernel differs from the printed one.
issues.title: The kernel in eq:kernel is not the Wendland function: it is negative on [0,1/4), discontinuous at 0, and makes close agents repel
issues.why_classification: The correction is a single forced character that restores the cited kernel and every substantive claim; no inference, construction, or guarantee is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: One should ensure that the compact set $E$ is large enough to allow both global interactions, i.e. $\phi(r_{ij}^\varepsilon)>0$ for any $i,j = 1,\ldots,N$, and no interactions at all, i.e. $\phi(r_{ij}^\varepsilon)=0$ for all $i,j = 1,\ldots,N$.

r_{ij}^\varepsilon(t)
    = \frac{\varepsilon_x(t)}{2}\bigl[(x_j-x_i)^2+(y_j-y_i)^2\bigr]
      + \frac{\varepsilon_c(t)}{2}\bigl(c_j(t)-c_i(t)\bigr)^2
For analytical convenience, we assume that the image is continuous in both space and intensity, and we rescale it so that $(x_i,y_i) \in \Omega := [0,1]^2$ for all pixels.

issues.failure_explanation: With Omega = [0,1]^2, the farthest pixel pair has squared spatial distance 2, so r_ij >= (eps_x/2)*2 = eps_x; since the kernel vanishes for r > 1, global interactions (phi(r_ij) > 0 for any i,j) require eps_x < 1 (and eps_c < 2), i.e. the control set must reach values below 1. The chosen set E = [2,1100]^2 has eps_x >= 2, so for every admissible control the farthest pair satisfies r_ij >= 2 > 1 and never interacts; the global-interaction regime required by Remark rmk:parameters is not achievable, contradicting the claim that the choice is made 'in accordance with' the remark.

failure_location.quote: In accordance with Remark~\ref{rmk:parameters}, we set $E = [2,1100]^2$ and initialise the control as $\varepsilon_x^{(0)} = \varepsilon_c^{(0)} \equiv 57$ at all discrete times.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Extend E to include values below 1 (e.g. [0.1,1100]^2 or [0,1100]^2) or relax the remark's requirement; a local parameter adjustment with no effect on the formal results.
issues.overall_effect: The control cannot reach the full-interaction regime that the paper's own parameter-selection criterion demands; the optimal controls are restricted to spatially local interactions only, which may bias the diffusion-versus-no-diffusion comparison between the two algorithms.
issues.title: The control set E = [2,1100]^2 cannot achieve the global-interaction regime that Remark rmk:parameters requires
issues.why_classification: A local parameter/regime adjustment suffices; no theorem, rate, or guarantee depends on the exact choice of E.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: There exists a saddle point for the functional $L : H^1(\Omega) \times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) \times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) \to \R$ defined in \eqref{eq:cost_tv_regular}.
L(u,v,\mu) = \int_\Omega |v(x)| + \mu(x) \cdot (v(x) - \nabla u(x)) + \frac{\rho}{2} |v(x) - \nabla u(x)|^2 + \frac{\alpha}{2}(u(x)- I(x))^2\ dx.

In general, the saddle point is not unique. In fact, when approaching the minimum point $(u^*,v^*)$ in the primal variables (which is unique), the term $\int_\Omega \mu \cdot (v^*-\nabla u^*)$ vanishes, so that any $\mu \in L^2(\Omega; \R^2)$ becomes feasible.

issues.failure_explanation: (i) The asserted joint coercivity on the product space is false: for fixed mu, take u_k a triangular spike of height 1/2 and slope +/-k on a strip of width 1/k (so ||u_k||_{L^2} is bounded, ||grad u_k||_{L^1} = 1, but ||grad u_k||_{L^2} = sqrt(k) -> infinity) and set v_k = grad u_k in L^2; then the penalty (rho/2)||v_k - grad u_k||^2 and the linear term vanish, so L(u_k, v_k, mu) = 1 + (alpha/2)||u_k - I||^2 stays bounded while ||(u_k,v_k)||_{H^1 x L^2} >= ||v_k||_{L^2} = sqrt(k) -> infinity. Hence the minimum need not be attained in a weakly compact subset of the stated space (minimizing sequences can escape toward BV or oscillate), and the cited saddle-point existence theory does not apply as invoked. (ii) A saddle point in the stated spaces forces v* = grad u* a.e. (otherwise sup_mu L = +infinity) with u* the ROF minimizer, which requires grad u* in L^2, i.e. u* in H^1; but ROF minimizers are in general only BV functions with measure-valued gradient, and no hypothesis on I ensuring this regularity is stated or proved. The existence claim is therefore unproven and fails in the stated spaces for general data.

failure_location.quote: Finally, as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:existence1}, it is immediate to show coercivity in the primal variables, ensuring that the minimum is attained in a weakly compact set.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reformulate the primal space (u in L^2 or BV with v a vector measure and mu in the appropriate dual) or add an explicit regularity hypothesis on I ensuring the ROF minimizer is in H^1, and reprove attainment by standard convex duality; the strong-duality content used by ADMM survives in the corrected spaces.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem thm:saddle_point, its strong-duality conclusion eq:duality (invoked to justify ADMM's 'no duality gap'), and the claimed attainment/uniqueness of the primal minimizer are unsupported as stated; the discretized Algorithm alg:admm is not itself invalidated.
issues.title: Saddle-point theorem: the claimed joint coercivity on H^1 x L^2 is false and existence requires unestablished H^1 regularity of the ROF minimizer
issues.why_classification: The repair is contained (change of function spaces or an added regularity hypothesis plus a standard duality argument) and preserves the duality content ADMM relies on, but the statement as written is unproven and can fail, so more than a local condition is needed.
